title: Apple iPhones Set for Limited Changes, Says Analyst - Barron's
text:
Apple iPhones Won’t See Major Redesigns in 2019, Says Analyst By Dec. 7, 2018 4:31 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Stuart C. Wilson/Getty Images Text size
With Apple (AAPL) stock down significantly in recent weeks due to worries about weak demand for the iPhone models released this fall, some investors are already looking forward to 2019’s offerings. Register for Our Webinar on Economic Uncertainty
Join us on Dec. 8 for a live conversation about economic uncertainly and where we go from here. We’ll discuss a range of issues—the trade war, oil prices, Brexit—and we’ll answer questions from listeners.
But Nomura analyst Anne Lee, who covers the greater China handset sector, is telling clients that the typical two-year cycle for big form-factor changes will not happen next year.
“We think the three new iPhones in 2H19F will likely have the same form factors (body size and displays) as the 2H18 iPhone XR, XS, and XS Max, with some added AR [augmented reality]-related features,” she wrote in a research report published Friday. As Microsoft moves closer to unseating Apple as the world’s most valuable company, the WSJ’s Dan Gallagher looks at the company’s steady rise over the last 10 years. Photo: Associated Press
As a result of the potential “limited changes” Lee estimates Apple iPhone unit sales will drop to 204 million in fiscal 2019 from 213 million in fiscal 2018, and then falling again to 200 million in fiscal 2020.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Its stock is down 3.5% to $168.65 on Friday.
“We think 2019 could be the last year the iPhone uses the iPhone X design architecture, in preparation for initial hardware specs for 5G (sub-6GHz) and AR (augmented reality), before greater architecture upgrades in 2020F for 5G and a more comprehensive AR system,” Lee wrote.
5G stands for fifth-generation wireless technology, which will enable much faster transmission speeds and new applications.
Morgan Stanley also forecasted lower iPhone shipments on Friday due to deteriorating demand in China. The firm’s analyst Katy Huberty lowered her price target to $236 from $253 for Apple stock, predicting that more consumers in the Asian country will hold on to their iPhones longer before upgrading to newer models.
